claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength together with favorable plasticity and machinability.
The balance of plasticity, machinability, hardness, and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is governed by the extent of nanoscale chemical short-range order.
Low CSRO permits relatively free dislocation motion.
Relatively free dislocation motion produces high plasticity and machinability.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by enhanced CSRO increases hardness and strength while reducing ductility.
Rapid solidification or quenching produces equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with minimal CSRO.
Moderate-temperature annealing for increasing durations can promote nanoscale CSRO without producing secondary-phase precipitates.
Increased local atomic ordering impedes both dislocation glide and cross-slip.
CSRO-related pinning increases hardness and strength through dislocation pile-up.
CSRO-promoting annealed samples will have higher hardness and compressive strength than untreated rapidly quenched samples.
CSRO-promoting annealed samples will have lower ductility than untreated rapidly quenched samples.
The predicted CSRO-dependent property differences will persist across 25–600 °C.
The hypothesis is limited to compression or hardness loading from approximately 25 °C to 600 °C while CoCrFeNiTi remains a single-phase solid solution.
Secondary-phase transformations or dominant grain-boundary phenomena may invalidate the proposed CSRO-controlled relationship.
